🔸A peace that never made it to the calendar🔸 ✍ Mohsen Hesam Mazaheri [Part 2 and Final] 4 The formation of calendars and their changes are not without reason. No occasion is remembered by chance and turned into a memory; just as no occasion is forgotten by accident. Which occasions and which figures are summoned from the depths of history and which are relegated to the archives depends on the needs and exigencies of society. More than having a historical root, it carries sociological significance and is influenced by the requirements, experiences, and necessities of society, as well as being the outcome of the will of power institutions at any given moment. If an event or a figure is recorded in the calendar, it is because it has a bearing on today and is meant to address a need in society or in power. And likewise, if it is not, it means its presence was not necessary. It is for this reason that by examining the course of changes in societies' calendars (both official and unofficial), one can understand them and the path of their transformations. 5 With this in mind, the very fact that today's conventional Shia, for example, knows the day of Lady Masoumeh's arrival in Qom and honors it, or holds mourning ceremonies for the passing of Lady Ruqayyah, but does not recognize the peace day of their second Imam, can explain a part of our present. 6 Of course, who knows. Perhaps one day the peace of Imam Hasan will be added to the Shia calendar, just as in our time there are not few occasions that have been added to ritual calendars without having been honored by Shias of earlier eras. The calendar is a living entity, just like society. 1405/06/18 @mohsenhesammazaheri

#New_Book_Releases_ArmaOn the eve of the 47th anniversary of Ayatollah Taleghani's passing, published:📔Payk-e Aftab📔A Study of the Record and Intellectual Legacy of Ayatollah Seyyed Mahmoud Taleghani(Third Edition)✍️ Mohammad EsfandiariFirst printing — Shahrivar 1405Roqai — 497 pagesThis book is a study of the era, life, thoughts, and works of Ayatollah Taleghani; a rare man who did not live for himself, never became confined to his own limitations, and devoted the capital of his life to the revival of humanity and humaneness. Among figures outside the religious sphere, Taleghani resembled Socrates and Gandhi. In epistemology, like Socrates, he believed that we know less than we think we do, and therefore we must learn from one another through dialogue, questioning, and answering. But in politics, he was like Gandhi; as hard as stone against the enemy and as soft as silk with a friend. In the two halves of the 20th century, two spiritual-political figures shone, each adorning humanity: Gandhi and Taleghani. The world knew and honored Gandhi, but alas, it did not know Taleghani and remained deprived. His compatriots, too, who found him in the heat of the revolution, lost him in the storm of subsequent events.Distribution: QoqnoosOnline purchase: IranKetab and CBook websites@nashre_arma
